basis: New mission, no workbook source. Facts: Taiwan 2024 generation ~11.6% renewables with wind generation +66% 2023->2024 (variability now a material grid share); 3 March 2022 cascading blackout triggered by a single switch malfunction at Hsinta Power Plant, Kaohsiung, cutting power to ~5.49M households (~40% of Taiwan) via cascading grid protection trips (Taiwan News/Bloomberg/CommonWealth); TSMC ~9% of national electricity, semiconductor/data-centre demand rising and less predictable (SDxCentral/TrendForce); Taipower reached ~1GW (1,000MW) of grid-connected battery storage in 2025, incl. the Dongshan 60MW site (operating Nov 2024) and a 20MW system at the Tainan salt-field solar farm (Taipower press releases); Taipower AMI/smart-meter rollout passed 3.5M customers (>80% of consumption) by May 2025, target 6M by 2030 and full replacement by 2035, plus a DER Integration program under Taipower's Smart Grid effort; Taiwan storage market ~1GW/3GWh and >1% of global electrochemical storage by 2025, projected toward 20GWh by 2030, market value ~US$3.1bn (2025) toward ~US$9.8bn (2031) (Infolink-group, Mobility Foresights); LFP batteries ~90% of new grid-scale storage worldwide, trading energy density for thermal stability, longer cycle life (thousands of cycles, 10-15+ years) and lower cost versus NMC/NCA chemistries used in EVs; private-sector example of a Fluence-partnered 100-MW-class storage project. slides.1: At night the sun disappears, and some days the wind barely blows at all. Batteries and smart grids increasingly provide the answer to where our electricity then comes from.
slides.2: SDG 7 is not only about clean power generation, but also about power that keeps working reliably whatever the weather. This talk focuses on keeping a grid that depends on the weather running.
slides.3: Taiwan's power grid has already wobbled once before this. In 2022, a single switch failure triggered a cascade that cut power to millions of households across the island.
slides.4: Renewable power now makes up a growing share of the grid. Wind generation alone has increased by about 66 percent in just one year, which makes supply much harder to forecast.
slides.5: In 2022, one broken switch in the south triggered a chain reaction across three regional grids. Almost 5.5 million households lost power within a short window that day.
slides.6: Chip factories now draw huge and rising amounts of electricity, and one factory alone uses close to 9 percent of the national total. Our grid was never designed for loads like this.
slides.7: Taipower has now reached about one full gigawatt of battery storage connected to the grid. One site, at Dongshan, started running in November 2024, clearly showing the idea works at real scale.
slides.8: Taipower has installed smart meters for over 3.5 million customers, reaching more than 80 percent of all power use. That real-time data is exactly what a smart grid needs.
slides.9: Taiwan's whole storage market has grown from a tiny niche into a business worth billions of dollars. One forecast expects it to keep expanding sharply all the way through 2030.
slides.10: Instead of the dense chemistry used in electric cars, most new grid batteries now use a chemistry called LFP. This trades away some range for safety and a longer working life.
slides.11: LFP battery cells last through thousands of charging cycles and rarely ever catch fire. That combination matters more for a fixed grid battery than raw energy density ever could.
slides.12: Instead of only building new power plants, Taipower's smart grid software now routes power in near real time. Rooftop solar, home batteries and even electric cars could soon join that same system.
slides.13: More sensors and more connected software also create more doors that a hacker could try. If a smart grid's control system is compromised, the damage could spread quickly.
slides.14: This growing storage industry is good news for Taiwan's tech sector. But someone still has to pay for all these batteries and meters, usually through higher electricity rates.
slides.15: Wealthier households can usually afford smart meters, home batteries and electric cars first. Poorer households may have to wait far longer, and that gap could widen if nobody plans ahead.
slides.16: So the very tools that solve one problem can quietly create new ones. A smart grid must also be genuinely judged on safety, fairness and who actually gets access to it.
slides.17: To wrap up, engineers are rebuilding Taiwan's grid piece by piece while it keeps running. New batteries, sensors and software now sit right alongside wiring and plants that are already decades old.
slides.18: This whole issue is not abstract for anyone in this room. You represent the next generation of engineers who will shape the batteries, algorithms and safety systems still to come.
slides.19: Learn to see the whole complicated system, not only one small technical component. Keep asking who gets these smart new tools first, and who is left waiting behind them.
slides.20: Let's build a grid that is not only clean but also genuinely reliable and fair for everyone. Every switch you flip belongs to a system you can now help shape.
